section_1.title: Prerequisites: Visualizing Planarity
section_1.content: Define a planar graph as one that can be drawn in a 2D plane without edges crossing. Introduce the concept of a 'Face' (f)—the enclosed regions, including the unbounded exterior region.
section_1.example: Visualizing a house shape (a square with a triangle on top) as a planar graph: 5 vertices, 6 edges, and 2 interior faces + 1 exterior face = 3 faces.

section_2.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
section_2.content: Introduce the fundamental theorem for connected planar graphs: V - E + F = 2. Explain how vertices (V), edges (E), and faces (F) maintain this constant balance, acting as a structural invariant.
section_2.example: Apply the formula to a simple cube graph flattened into a 2D plane: 8 vertices - 12 edges + 6 faces = 2.

section_3.title: The Concept of Dual Graphs
section_3.content: Explain the construction of a dual graph: place a point (vertex) inside every face of the original graph, and connect two points if their corresponding faces share an edge.
section_3.example: Imagine a map of a kingdom: each 'territory' (face) becomes a city (dual vertex), and shared borders become 'roads' (dual edges).

section_4.title: Interplay: Duality and Euler
section_4.content: Demonstrate that the dual of a dual graph returns the original structure. Connect this to the variables: V_dual = F, F_dual = V, and E_dual = E. Explain why duality preserves the Euler Characteristic.
section_4.example: Using an animation showing a 'Starry Constellation' (original graph) transforming into a 'Network of Cities' (dual graph), then mapping back, visually verifying the symmetry.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize how these concepts are used in VLSI circuit design and map coloring. Wrap up with the 'invariant' nature of topology.
section_5.example: A microchip designer uses the dual graph to route power lines; Euler's formula acts as a sanity check to ensure the layout remains planar and efficient.
